title: "Containers For Scientific Computing"
output: html_document
---

Containers should be used as a standard in scientific computing, especially for 
those projects aiming to make "An App for That". Or as I like to say Jaffas, 
*just another f__ing fone app".  

Containers are frameworks which are light weight and can run on any platform, 
Mac, linux or windows without the need to adjust the software for the operating 
system. 
The also can ensure that all the software on which your application or code 
relies on is packaged with your app. 
That way if the maintainer of one small piece of your code decides to make a 
[breaking change](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/21703216/what-is-a-breaking-change-in-software)
then your containerised app will still work when a non-containerised app with 
updated dependencies will not work.  

<br>

### Why bother with containers?  

Software dependencies make scientific work more prone to failure. 
This is perfectly summarised by the phrase, "more moving parts has more points 
of failure". 
When scientific research is predominantly contract based for a specific time 
period this can ensure that as soon as the funding stops, the apps stop working 
as well.  


<center>
![xkcd comic 2347: Dependency](https://imgs.xkcd.com/comics/dependency.png)  
</center>

<br>

Another problem is the aspect of 'reproducibility' or 
"It works on my machine"  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯. 
As mentioned earlier, containers are portable to different operating systems improving reproducibility.

The most recognised container software is called 
[Docker](https://www.docker.com/), yet there are other container software out 
there which might be more suitable and have wider usage, eg. 
[containerd](https://containerd.io/). 
In this blog I will use `docker` as I am the most familiar with this software.
